Manufacturing Process Complexity and  
Environmental Impact
Many of the major trends in semiconductor manufacturing 
have helped reduce environmental impact over time. For 
example, the industry’s move from 200-millimeter (mm) to 
300mm	wafers	increased	manufacturing	energy	efficiency	by	about	20%,	primarily	
because more chips could be produced at a time. The trend toward smaller chips, such as 
the Intel® Atom™ processor, generates savings for similar reasons, as do advancements 
through Moore’s Law that enable the sizes of features on chips to shrink over time.
However, innovation also creates some challenges in the areas of water conservation 
and chemical waste reduction, due in part to the increasing complexity of our 
manufacturing processes and the additional manufacturing steps used to create 
our newer microprocessors. This complexity can be understood by comparing our 
manufacturing process to building a city. We used to be able to build outward, the way 
that cities expand into suburban areas. We are now also “building up,” as cities do by 
constructing skyscrapers. The multi-layered, vertical nature of our newer technology 
creates	more	powerful	and	energy-efficient	products,	but	it	also	requires	increased	use	
of chemicals and water rinses. In addition, we have been driving chemical and water use 
reductions	for	well	over	two	decades,	so	many	available	efficiencies	have	already	been	
realized,	making	it	difficult	to	achieve	additional	large	reductions.	However,	we	remain	
committed	to	finding	innovative	ways	to	further	reduce	our	operational	environmental	
impact	and	to	applying	our	energy-efficient	technology	and	expertise	to	help	customers,	
communities, and cities around the world become more sustainable.
